articles.title: Aoki: Infostealer Targets AI Coding Assistant Credentials
articles.context: Earlier versions of the malware did not target AI-related files, which indicates the capability is a recent addition
articles.full_text:
Key findings

The Aoki (aka Aokigahara) infostealer is now stealing credential and session files used by AI coding assistants, including Claude, OpenAI's Codex, Cursor, Codeium and Gemini. Earlier versions of the malware did not target AI-related files, which indicates the capability is a recent addition.

Stolen application programming interface (API) keys and tokens can allow attackers to carry out activity under a legitimate user's identity and API quota. The tokens can also expose connected repositories, cloud services and continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines linked to the account.

The most up-to-date sample of this malware analyzed by the Symantec Threat Hunter team also stole data from dozens of browsers, cryptocurrency wallets, password managers, messaging and gaming applications, and VPN and FTP clients.

The malware has no backdoor command list. It collects whatever data is available and sends it to its command-and-control (C&C) server.

The Aoki (aka Aokigahara) infostealer has begun stealing credentials for AI coding assistants. Recent versions of Aoki analyzed by the Symantec Threat Hunter team were designed to harvest credential and session files for Claude, OpenAI's Codex, Cursor, Codeium and Gemini, alongside the browser, cryptocurrency wallet and password manager data that infostealers typically collect.

The capability is recent and appears to be expanding. Aoki is a relatively new stealer that was first seen earlier in 2026. However, older samples did not look for AI-related files, meaning the capability was added to the malware recently.

The newest version of the threat found by the Threat Hunter Team targeted .claude.json, Claude desktop cookies, ChatGPT cookies, and the Codex config.toml and .env files. In addition, it stole tokens for GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Google Gemini, JetBrains AI Assistant and Kiro, along with Amazon Web Services (AWS) credentials.

Wider data theft

As well as the AI-related targets, Aoki attempts to steal a wide range of other information from victim machines, including:

Cookies, autofill data, credit card information, history and Google tokens from the following browsers: Chrome; Edge; Brave; Opera; Opera GX; Opera Neon; Vivaldi; Yandex; 360; CentBrowser; Coc Coc; Comodo Dragon; Epic; Iridium; Torch; Slimjet; URBrowser; SRWare Iron; 7Star; Amigo; Sputnik; Atom; Orbitum; QQ; Whale; Maxthon; Avast/AVG/CCleaner browsers; Kinza; Sidekick; Arc; Thorium; DuckDuckGo; Ghostery; Lunascape; Mercury; Edge WebView2; Firefox; Waterfox; LibreWolf; Pale Moon; Basilisk; SeaMonkey, and Floorp.

Wallet browser extensions, including: MetaMask; MetaMask (Edge); Phantom; TronLink; Coinbase; Binance; Trust; Exodus; Brave; Ronin; Solflare; Slope; Rabby; Terra Station; Keplr; Sollet; Coin98; XDEFI; KardiaChain; Nami; Maiar; Temple; Yoroi; Guarda; EVER; Jaxx Liberty; BitPay; Wombat; Oxygen; Crocobit; Finnie; Kaikas; BOLT X; Liquality; Leaf; Clover; Math; GeroWallet; HashPack; Talisman; SubWallet; Polkadot{.js}; Martian; Pontem; Petra; Fewcha; OKX; Sender; TokenPocket; Backpack; Sui; Enkrypt; Core; Zerion; Rainbow; Frontier; Blade; Bitget; Compass; 1inch; Fluent; Braavos; ArgentX; Fractal; Tonkeeper; UniSat; Leather; SafePal, and Rise.

Desktop wallets, including: Exodus; Atomic; Electrum; Electrum-LTC; Ethereum keystore; Zcash; Armory; Bytecoin; Jaxx; Guarda; Coinomi; Wasabi; Dogecoin; Dash; Litecoin; Bitcoin Core; Monero; Daedalus; Binance; Ledger Live, and TokenPocket.

It also looks for files with the following in the name: mnemonic; recovery; privatekey; private_key; passphrase; backup; keystore; secret; 12word; 24word, wallet or phrase.

Steals Discord tokens from Discord, PTB, Canary, Development and Lightcord.

Steals Discord tokens and files from Vesktop; Legcord; Equicord; ArmCord; WebCord; Dorion; Abaddon; GoofCord; Spacebar; Vencord; BetterDiscord; Replugged, and OpenAsar.

Steals from Telegram-related messaging services such as tdata; 64Gram; AyuGram; Kotatogram; Nekogram; Extragram; iMe, and Unigram.

Steals gaming-related files for Steam; Roblox; Epic Games; Battle.net; Riot; Minecraft; GOG; Origin, and Ubisoft.

Steals Outlook passwords from the registry and Mozilla Thunderbird profiles.

Steals saved information from file transfer programs, including: FileZilla; WinSCP; CoreFTP; FlashFXP, and SmartFTP.

Steals information from OpenVPN; NordVPN; ProtonVPN; PIA; Surfshark, and Windscribe.

Steals from password managers, including: KeePass config; Bitwarden; 1Password; Dashlane; RoboForm; NordPass, and Sticky Password.

It also records which security products are installed on a machine.

Aoki collects the available data from victim machines and sends it to its C&C server, using a /gate endpoint. Most of the newer samples used one domain, while two newer samples used a domain of their own. Older samples used an IP address and port 8080 over unencrypted HTTP.

Why AI credentials are valuable

API keys and Open Authorization (OAuth) or session tokens allow malicious activity to be carried out under a legitimate developer's identity and API quota. They can also expose connected repositories, cloud services and CI/CD pipelines linked to that account, and may bypass safeguards that assume requests originate from a trusted user.

The malware stole credential, token and session files rather than source code. The exception is the local state database used by Cursor, which can cache chat context and code snippets.

A little-documented family

The name of this infostealer comes from a longer name (Aokigahara) in a string used by the malware during its decryption process. While there has been some limited publication about this malware, its functionality has not been extensively documented, and its targeting of AI assistants is a new development that hasn’t previously been reported. We do not know what threat group may be behind this malware and there are no indications that it has links to any existing malware family.

Aokigahara is the name of a very famous forest in Japan, but it’s not clear if that provides any clues as to the origins of the malware’s developers.

Significance

While payment card data and cryptocurrency wallets have long been a mainstay for information stealing malware, this development suggests AI credentials may be considered just as valuable for attackers. Like card data, a stolen AI key can be cashed in directly, either through resale or by running up usage on the victim's account, a practice sometimes called LLMjacking. Unlike card data, it can also give an attacker a route into the developer's wider environment.

The rest of Aoki's target list points to a financial motive, with a strong focus on cryptocurrency-related wallets and extensions. The attackers are also clearly interested in credentials and accessing information about victims from the likes of Telegram and Discord sessions, which could potentially also give them access to other victims in the form of the victims’ contacts.

Aoki is a highly-capable and multi-functional infostealer whose capabilities still appear to be in active development.

Protection

If an IOC is malicious and the file is available to us, Symantec Endpoint products will detect and block that file. Symantec detects this family as Infostealer.Aoki.
